title: Type I for Organizations: Nine Ways to Improve Your Company, Office, or Group
coreMove: Organizations move toward engagement by redesigning autonomy, recognition, feedback, and purpose rather than decorating control.

exampleSpecs.audience: Cora, an operations director auditing autonomy before blaming morale
exampleSpecs.stakes: A quarterly review is about to treat disengagement as an attitude problem.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use an autonomy audit as an environmental diagnosis.

exampleSpecs.audience: Desmond, a product lead designing a bounded hack day
exampleSpecs.stakes: A hack day needs real autonomy and a real delivery moment.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show FedEx Day freedom inside a container.

exampleSpecs.audience: Inez, a facilitator making recognition useful
exampleSpecs.stakes: Peer recognition could become popularity theater or genuine feedback.

exampleSpecs.audience: Ravi, a nonprofit leader testing whose purpose is shared
exampleSpecs.stakes: A retreat may reveal that the mission is executive language, not a common guide.

exampleSpecs.audience: Selah, a people lead pairing flexibility with outcomes
exampleSpecs.stakes: A hybrid-work policy needs trust and standards at the same time.

exampleSpecs.audience: Bram, a customer success manager revising a harmful metric
exampleSpecs.stakes: A metric rewards visibility while punishing good judgment.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Change one measure that teaches the wrong motive.
